newsitem.title: FRANCE: French fans see rugby final, taste political future.
newsitem.headline: French fans see rugby final, taste political future.

text.p: Fans watching the French Rugby Union championship final on Saturday night got an early taste of the country's possible political future -- tense "cohabitation" (power-sharing).

Millions of television viewers saw French President Jacques Chirac sharing the VIP second of the stands with the two men best-placed to become his next prime minister after Sunday's parliamentary election runoff.

Socialist party chief Lionel Jospin was banished to the far end of the front row, but Chirac's fellow-Gaullist Philippe Seguin sat at the president's left for the clash between Bourgoin-Jallieu and Stade Toulousain.

In case voters had any doubts as to where Chirac's preferences lay, the head of state invited Seguin to dinner at the Elysee presidential palace before the two travelled together to the evening match.
Before play started, Chirac walked down to the pitch to shake hands and chat with the players in a well-orchestrated media event -- virtually his last handshakes of the campaign.

Seguin, on cool terms with the president since being passed over for premier two years ago, is widely touted by media as the man Chirac will name as government chief if the centre-right wins the election.
Jospin was also in the official stand because one of the two teams in the final, Stade Toulousain, is based close to his constituency in southwestern France.
Chirac's office confirmed press reports that Jospin had called them about seating, requesting that he not be placed near scandal-tarnished Paris mayor Jean Tiberi, a former Chirac aide.
Chirac and Jospin sat on either side of the late President Francois Mitterrand two years ago at the same championship event on the eve of Chirac's election over Jospin to replace Mitterrand.
